q: Is pNDM5-SCNJ1 genuinely the first NDM-5-in-ST29 K. pneumoniae, or is the paper's earlier IncX3 hit (pQDE2-NDM, MH917280, 100% coverage / 99.99% identity, K. pneumoniae isolate 2015 Shandong) actually the same plasmid in an ST29 host that was never MLST-typed at the isolate level?
basis: Yuan et al. explicitly claim 'blaNDM-5 is described for the first time in a strain of K. pneumoniae ST29 in our work' (Results & Discussion, p.3), yet their own IncX3 tree (Fig. 5, Table S4) lists pQDE2-NDM as 100% coverage / 99.99% identity to pNDM5-SCNJ1 — essentially the same plasmid, present in a K. pneumoniae isolate three years earlier in the same country. The paper never checks whether that 2015 host was ST29. Our replication verified the plasmid-level identity (Mash distance ~0.00007 in our IncX3 NJ tree) but did not resolve the host ST because MH917280 is a plasmid-only accession. If the host is ST29, the 'first' claim collapses.
next_steps: 1) Locate the source publication behind MH917280 (Shandong 2015 K. pneumoniae isolate); scrape BioProject/BioSample metadata for the host isolate accession. 2) If the host WGS is public, run Kleborate MLST to confirm the ST. 3) If not public, email the corresponding authors of MH917280 for the ST typing of the host or for the isolate reads. 4) Extend to all IncX3-pNDM5-carrying K. pneumoniae isolates in NCBI 2015-present, MLST-type every host that has a WGS, and produce a corrected timeline of first-in-ST29 events. Deliverable: a claim-audit note that either confirms or overturns the 'first' claim.

q: How robust is the paper's 'ancestral vector' inference that IncX3-pEC14_35 (JN935899, 1989 USA, no resistance genes) is the backbone ancestor of the modern blaNDM-5-carrying IncX3 clade? Their argument is purely structural (shared backbone) and does not use a time-calibrated phylogeny; is the temporal / biogeographic gap actually consistent with molecular-clock rates for narrow-host-range plasmids?
basis: The paper argues (p.5, Fig.4b) that pEC14_35 (1989, USA) is 'likely to be the ancestral vector' and that pNDM5-SCNJ1 diverged from blaNDM-1-positive pBJ01 'by sequential mutations.' This is a topological / structural argument only — no dated tree, no clock model, no ancestral state reconstruction, and no test against alternative acquisition scenarios (independent NDM-5 recombination events, mobile-element-mediated shuffling). Our IncX3 NJ tree (231 plasmids, Mash) reproduces the topology but is also inherently untimed, so we cannot check the claim either. A dated phylogeny using core-backbone SNPs and Bayesian tip-dating could either support or refute the ancestral-vector inference.
next_steps: 1) Extract the 30-kb conserved backbone (pir, bis, parA, hns, topB, conjugation cluster) from all 231 IncX3 plasmids. 2) Build an alignment; call backbone SNPs excluding the genetic-load region. 3) Run BEAST2 or TreeTime tip-dating using GenBank sequencing years as tip dates. 4) Reconstruct ancestral states at internal nodes; test whether pEC14_35 falls near the MRCA or is a derived branch. 5) Estimate substitution rate and test whether the observed backbone diversity is consistent with a single 1980s origin vs multiple independent captures. 6) Publish or push to a preprint the corrected evolutionary model — the current 'ancestral vector' claim is a widely cited but never-quantified assertion.

q: The paper reports 198 core-SNP distance between SCNJ1 and its closest ST29 relative SCLZ15-011 (CSI Phylogeny, unfiltered). Our replication with Parsnp+Gubbins yields 53 SNPs — a 3.7x reduction. Which value is right, and what fraction of published K. pneumoniae SNP-distance-based transmission/outbreak claims are inflated by non-recombination-filtered pipelines?
basis: The paper does not report a recombination-filtering step for the pairwise SNP counts (Gubbins is only mentioned as being applied to the RAxML tree input, not to the pairwise distance reporting). Our post-Gubbins alignment removed 368,803 bp of recombinant regions before the pairwise count. In our REPORT.md we hand-waved the discrepancy as 'methodological difference' and moved on — that is unsatisfying because a factor of ~4 discrepancy in SNP distances is the difference between 'unrelated' and 'putative transmission chain' in outbreak epidemiology. We never actually re-ran CSI Phylogeny on the same inputs to reproduce the 198 value; if the paper is systematically 4x-inflated, downstream Chinese-hospital outbreak calls based on similar pipelines are also inflated.
next_steps: 1) Actually re-run CSI Phylogeny 1.4 (or its successor) on our SCNJ1 + 59 ST29 assemblies with the paper's stated parameters and confirm we reproduce 198 SNPs (this closes the reproducibility gap). 2) Repeat with and without a Gubbins post-filter on the same input to isolate the recombination-inflation factor. 3) Sample 20 recent K. pneumoniae outbreak papers that cite pairwise SNP thresholds (<25, <50 SNPs) for transmission calls; audit whether they filtered recombination. 4) Publish a short methods note quantifying the systematic bias and proposing a standardized reporting requirement (post-Gubbins distance MUST be reported alongside raw).

q: The paper's rmpA2 truncation is described as a 'frameshift mutation introducing an internal stop codon' but the exact nucleotide coordinates, the causal indel, and whether the truncation is convergent across the KpVP-1/pLVPK-family or represents a specific pVir-SCNJ1 lesion are never reported. Is this a single-lineage lesion or a systematic pattern in ST29/K54 virulence plasmids, and does it affect hypermucoviscosity phenotype quantitatively?
basis: Yuan et al. state (Results & Discussion, p.4) that rmpA2 is 'truncated, due to a frameshift mutation introducing an internal stop codon,' full stop — no coordinates, no comparison to a functional reference (e.g. pLVPK rmpA2), no test of whether closely-related pVir plasmids share the same truncation. Kleborate calls rmpA2 at 60% (our replication) which suggests the truncation is real but does not localize it. This matters because (a) rmpA2 vs rmpA vs rmpADC copy number and integrity is a known modifier of hypermucoviscosity magnitude, and (b) if the same truncation is present in multiple KpVP-1 plasmids it suggests a conserved regulatory tuning rather than a random loss.
next_steps: 1) Extract the exact rmpA2 ORF from pVir-SCNJ1 (NZ_CP174530.1), align to the pLVPK rmpA2 reference (NC_005249), and localize the frameshift indel to a nucleotide position. 2) Run the same alignment against rmpA2 from all 30-40 publicly available KpVP-1 virulence plasmids; classify each as intact / truncated-at-position-X / other. 3) Test whether the truncation position is enriched in specific IncHI1/IncFIB lineages or geographic clusters. 4) Correlate with published hypermucoviscosity scores or string-test lengths for the corresponding isolates when metadata allow. 5) If a systematic pattern emerges, this is a candidate for a mechanistic follow-up: does the truncated rmpA2 retain partial regulatory function via the N-terminal domain, or is it a functional null?

q: The paper's dataset stops at March 2019 (accessed date given for the 6823 K. pneumoniae genomes and 230 IncX3 plasmids). Seven years later, has the ST29/K54/blaNDM-5/pNDM5-MGR194-like plasmid combination remained a Sichuan-China-restricted lineage, or has it spread internationally via IncX3-plasmid transfer into diverse ST backgrounds? A 2026-vintage re-sweep is entirely feasible with the same tools.
basis: Our replication reproduces the paper's phylogenies (60-genome ST29 tree; 231-plasmid IncX3 tree) using the same 2019-cutoff data, but we did not extend the corpus. The paper's own concluding sentence explicitly asks for 'more extensive surveillance.' The mash+abricate pipeline we used is trivially re-runnable on the current NCBI IncX3 plasmid set (likely 400-600+ plasmids by now) and the current ST29 K. pneumoniae WGS set (likely doubled since 2019). This is the highest-leverage next question because it directly tests whether the paper's warning was heeded, ignored, or was in fact overstated.
next_steps: 1) Re-pull all NCBI K. pneumoniae genomes as of 2026-07 and MLST-type; extract all ST29 isolates. 2) Re-pull all IncX3 plasmids (regardless of resistance gene) using PlasmidFinder against a fresh NCBI mirror. 3) Re-run the Parsnp+Gubbins+RAxML-NG pipeline on the extended ST29 set with SCNJ1 as an anchor; measure branch length accumulation since 2019. 4) Re-run Mash+NJ on the extended IncX3 set; identify new near-neighbors of pNDM5-SCNJ1. 5) For every new close-relative isolate, extract country/year metadata; produce a 2019→2026 spread map. 6) Estimate the emergence rate of ST29-blaNDM-5 co-occurrence per year; check whether the K54 capsular type is enriched in the extended set. Deliverable: a 'seven-year follow-up' short report suitable for a rapid-communication venue.
